positions.commentary: The speaker notes that in the past, buying IBM was not controversial enough to get an investor fired, implying it represents non-controversial businesses at ridiculous valuations.
The speaker criticizes META for making massive single bets which violates the rules of investing, contrasting it with small bets.
The speaker cites Microsoft as an example of a blue-chip stock where the 52-week range is well beyond 10%, illustrating the volatility of auction-driven markets.
The speaker mentions Amazon as an example of a blue-chip stock used to illustrate the wide price ranges found in auction-driven markets compared to negotiated transactions.
The speaker mentions Carvana as an example of a company that experienced crazy pricing and euphoria after its IPO, illustrating the volatility of auction-driven markets.

thesis: This episode uses examples of blue-chip stocks like IBM, MSFT, and AMZN to illustrate the volatility of auction-driven markets, contrasting them with negotiated transactions. It also critiques META for making massive single bets that violate investing rules, while noting that buying non-controversial businesses at ridiculous valuations (like IBM) is not a controversial strategy.
